name: Clustering Papers by Meaning
title: Clustering Papers by Meaning
answer: Clustering papers by meaning groups research documents according to what they argue, show, or investigate, rather than by surface features such as shared citations, author overlap, or keyword matches. It is used in citation mapping to reveal thematic clusters, emerging subfields, and overlooked connections across a corpus. The output is a set of clusters where each cluster contains papers that address a similar question, method, or finding, even if they do not cite one another. This supports literature review, research discovery, and gap analysis.

sections.body: Clustering papers by meaning groups research documents according to what they argue, show, or investigate, rather than by surface features such as shared citations, author overlap, or keyword matches. It is used in citation mapping to reveal thematic clusters, emerging subfields, and overlooked connections across a corpus. The output is a set of clusters where each cluster contains papers that address a similar question, method, or finding, even if they do not cite one another. This supports literature review, research discovery, and gap analysis.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a document store of full texts or abstracts, plus a vector index built from paper embeddings. A typical setup uses a transformer model to encode each paper into a dense vector, then stores those vectors in a local or cloud vector database. For a small library, such as the 135 papers held on this site, the whole pipeline can run on a single workstation with a CPU or a modest GPU. No external search tool is needed, and the site links to original papers rather than to a third-party search product.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The core method is to embed each paper's title, abstract, and, where available, full text into a shared vector space using a pretrained language model. Similarity between papers is then computed with cosine distance or a related metric. Clustering is applied to the resulting similarity matrix, often with algorithms such as hierarchical agglomerative clustering, k-means on reduced dimensions, or community detection on a nearest-neighbor graph. The number of clusters is usually chosen by inspecting a dendrogram or by setting a similarity threshold, not by assuming a fixed count in advance.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on how paper text is used for embeddings and how cluster labels are presented. If full text is processed, access must respect publisher terms, and the site's practice of linking to the original paper rather than to a search tool keeps provenance clear. A cluster label generated from embeddings can misstate a paper's argument, so human review of cluster membership and labels is part of responsible use. There is also a risk that clustering by meaning amplifies dominant framings and hides minority or critical work, so cluster boundaries should be treated as provisional.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward finer-grained clustering that separates a paper's claims, methods, and evidence rather than treating the whole paper as one unit. As embedding models improve, clusters will become more stable across paraphrases and languages, and interactive maps will let a researcher move between cluster view and the original paper. The site's extracted claims, currently 11,222 across its library, point toward claim-level clustering as a next step, where individual findings are grouped even when they come from papers in different fields.
